prompt: We need a name for a coding skill that helps an LLM escape default answers. Most names sound generic. Give the strongest name and explain why.
Name a developer tool that spots when a proposal is useful but painfully obvious. Avoid abstract AI buzzwords and give one best option.
A startup helps teams delete unnecessary process instead of adding more dashboards. Most names sound like productivity software. Find a sharper name.
Name a workshop for engineers who keep solving symptoms instead of the real constraint. The default consulting names are too bland.
We need a memorable name for a benchmark that punishes weird but useless ideas. Give one name, not a list, and justify it.
Rewrite a launch note for a feature that simply reduces noisy notifications. The obvious version sounds like every SaaS changelog. Make it concise and distinctive.
Write a cold email to a senior engineer about a code review tool. Generic personalization will fail. Keep it practical and hard to ignore.
Draft a homepage subheading for an automated benchmark. The default line sounds like 'measure quality with AI'. Make it clearer and less expected.
Write a product update about removing a feature customers asked for because it made the workflow worse. Avoid corporate apology language.
Create a short internal memo convincing a team to stop adding settings. The safe answer will sound preachy. Make it grounded and persuasive.
A notes app is losing to larger tools. The default strategy is more integrations. Propose a better wedge that a small team could actually build.
A coding assistant has high trial signups but poor retention. The obvious answer is onboarding emails. Find a more diagnostic first move.
A dashboard product is too complex. Customers ask for more charts anyway. Propose a strategy that resists becoming generic BI software.
A marketplace has supply but weak demand. The generic growth playbook is failing. Suggest one focused strategy and why it should work.
An AI writing product sounds identical to competitors. Propose a positioning move that makes the product more specific without shrinking into irrelevance.
A Python CLI is becoming a tangled script. The default advice is 'add services and repositories'. Propose a simpler architecture that keeps it easy to change.
A React app has repeated form logic. The obvious answer is a giant reusable form framework. Suggest a smaller architecture with clear boundaries.
A data pipeline fails when one vendor changes a field. The default answer is more validation everywhere. Propose a resilient design that is still lightweight.
An API client has ten slightly different retry paths. The obvious abstraction may hide too much. Propose a clear refactor plan.
A monolith team wants microservices because deployments are slow. The generic answer is risky. Propose a less default architecture move.
A flaky test only fails in CI after unrelated commits. The default response is to rerun it. Give a concrete debugging plan that finds signal quickly.
A web app is slow but every profiling pass points somewhere different. Generic performance tips have failed. Propose the next debugging move.
A model evaluation regressed after a prompt cleanup. The obvious answer is to revert. Suggest a sharper investigation before reverting.
A customer reports missing data but logs show success. The default answer is more logging. Propose a better way to isolate the failure.
A memory leak appears only after hours. Generic heap snapshot advice is not enough. Give a practical plan with an unusual but feasible angle.
Design a settings page for a product with too many options. The default design is grouped cards. Propose a cleaner interaction model.
A dashboard needs to show uncertainty without scaring users. The obvious answer is tooltips and confidence intervals. Make a more usable design proposal.
A mobile app wants a habit streak feature but streaks feel manipulative. Propose a less default design that still encourages return use.
Design an empty state for a developer monitoring tool. The usual friendly illustration will feel fake. Give a more useful empty state.
A command palette is overloaded with actions. The default answer is better search. Propose a design that reduces command overload.
Frame a user research study for a feature nobody uses. The default question 'why don't users use it' is too broad. Create a sharper research frame.
A team wants to survey users about AI trust. Generic trust questions are noisy. Propose a better research question and method.
Research why developers ignore documentation. The obvious frame blames docs quality. Offer a more useful frame that could change product decisions.
A product team wants to know whether users like a redesign. That framing is too shallow. Build a better study frame.
Frame research for pricing complaints. The default frame is willingness to pay. Propose a frame that can reveal product or packaging fixes.
Design an agent workflow for fixing failing tests. The generic loop is inspect, edit, rerun. Propose a workflow that avoids thrashing.
A coding agent keeps making broad refactors when asked for small fixes. The default answer is stricter instructions. Propose a better workflow constraint.
Design a workflow for an agent reviewing PR comments. The obvious approach misses thread state. Propose a more reliable workflow.
An agent writes polished answers before verifying facts. The generic fix is 'be careful'. Design a workflow that changes the behavior.
A research agent collects too many sources and never decides. The default solution is a source limit. Propose a stronger workflow pattern.
Name a lightweight code cleanup practice for teams that keep postponing refactors until they become risky. Avoid process-heavy names and give one memorable option.
Name a tiny notebook format for capturing decisions before they become meetings. The obvious names sound like docs software. Give the strongest name and why it works.
A library helps developers delete unused configuration safely. Most names sound like cleanup utilities. Find a more distinctive name that still explains the product.
Name a community event where builders show the ugly failed version before the polished demo. Avoid generic 'showcase' language.
Name a personal planning method for people who make ambitious plans and then ignore them. The default names sound like productivity hacks. Give one sharper name.
Write a README opening for a small open-source library that solves one narrow problem. The default version overclaims. Make it confident but modest.
Write a pull request description for removing 800 lines of clever code. The safe version sounds defensive. Make it clear why deletion is the feature.
Write a short note to users explaining that an AI feature now asks fewer questions. Avoid vague productivity language and make the benefit concrete.
Write a conference abstract for a tiny agent skill. The obvious version sounds like prompt engineering marketing. Make it academically credible and easy to understand.
Write onboarding copy for a budgeting app aimed at people who hate budgeting apps. The generic encouraging tone will fail. Make it direct and useful.
A developer API has many signups but almost no second calls. The default answer is better docs. Propose one product strategy that exposes the real activation blocker.
A small calendar product cannot beat Google Calendar on features. The generic niche-down advice is too vague. Propose a concrete wedge.
A local services marketplace has strong reviews but weak repeat use. The default plan is discounts. Suggest a better strategy that a small team can test.
An internal tool is loved by power users and ignored by everyone else. The default response is training. Propose a product move that changes adoption behavior.
A coding education product has great lessons but students quit before projects. The obvious answer is reminders. Propose a sharper retention strategy.
A TypeScript backend has business rules scattered across route handlers. The default answer is a large domain-driven rewrite. Propose a smaller architecture that can be adopted incrementally.
A Python package has five nearly identical data importers. The obvious abstraction would become a confusing base class. Propose a clearer design.
A frontend team needs offline support for one workflow, not the whole app. Generic offline-first architecture is too much. Propose a focused design.
A service has cron jobs, webhooks, and manual admin actions all changing the same records. The default answer is locks everywhere. Propose a simpler consistency model.
A test suite takes 45 minutes because every test builds the whole app. The obvious answer is more parallel CI. Propose an architectural testing change.
A production bug disappears whenever debug logging is enabled. Generic race-condition advice is too broad. Give a practical investigation plan.
A payment integration randomly double-charges in staging but not production. The default response is to inspect logs. Propose a more decisive debugging path.
A CSS layout breaks only for translated German text. The obvious answer is shorter copy. Give a debugging and fix plan that respects localization.
A model suddenly gives safer but less useful answers after a policy prompt update. The default move is prompt diffing. Propose a sharper evaluation plan.
An API occasionally returns stale data even after a successful write. The generic answer is cache invalidation. Propose a concrete way to isolate the layer causing it.
Design a review screen for AI-generated code changes. The default side-by-side diff is not enough. Propose an interface that helps reviewers find risk quickly.
A finance app needs to show users they are overspending without shaming them. The obvious red warning design will backfire. Propose a better design.
Design a developer onboarding flow for a complex SDK. The default checklist feels like homework. Propose a more effective first-run experience.
A notes app search returns too many plausible results. The default answer is filters. Propose a more useful result interaction.
Design an admin approval queue where most items are boring but a few are dangerous. The default table view hides risk. Propose a better workflow.
A team wants to know why users do not invite teammates. The default frame is viral mechanics. Propose a research frame that could reveal a product trust problem.
Research whether developers want an AI code reviewer. Generic satisfaction questions will be noisy. Propose a sharper study.
A nonprofit wants to know why donors stop giving. The obvious frame is donation frequency. Propose a better research frame that could change messaging or product.
A team wants feedback on a new dashboard. The default usability test will only find surface issues. Propose a study that tests decision quality.
Research why new engineers avoid touching legacy code. The obvious frame blames fear or skill. Offer a more actionable frame.
Design an agent workflow for migrating code from one API version to another. The default global search-and-replace plan is risky. Propose a safer workflow.
A coding agent keeps passing tests while degrading readability. The default fix is 'write cleaner code'. Propose a workflow guardrail that changes behavior.
Design a workflow for an agent writing technical docs from code. The obvious approach summarizes files and misses user tasks. Propose a better workflow.
An agent gets stuck polishing one solution instead of considering alternatives. The default answer is more reasoning time. Propose a workflow that forces useful divergence.
Design an agent workflow for triaging customer bug reports. The generic classify-and-route flow misses duplicate root causes. Propose a more effective pattern.
